claim: Crumbs is an evolutionarily conserved protein required for epithelial polarity and morphogenesis.
source: The evolutionarily conserved Crumbs protein is required for epithelial polarity and morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge about Crumbs function.

claim: Crumbs functions as a negative regulator of actomyosin dynamics during dorsal closure in the Drosophila embryo.
source: Here we identify a novel role of Crumbs as a negative regulator of actomyosin dynamics during dorsal closure in the Drosophila embryo.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Embryos carrying a mutation in the FERM domain-binding motif of Crumbs die due to an overactive actomyosin network associated with disrupted adherens junctions.
source: Embryos carrying a mutation in the FERM (protein 4.1/ezrin/radixin/moesin) domain-binding motif of Crumbs die due to an overactive actomyosin network associated with disrupted adherens junctions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations.

claim: The phenotype caused by mutation in the FERM domain-binding motif of Crumbs is restricted to the amnioserosa and does not affect other embryonic epithelia.
source: This phenotype is restricted to the amnioserosa and does not affect other embryonic epithelia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by observations in the results section.

claim: The function of Crumbs during dorsal closure requires DMoesin, the Rho1-GTPase, class-I p21-activated kinases and the Arp2/3 complex.
source: This function of Crumbs requires DMoesin, the Rho1-GTPase, class-I p21-activated kinases and the Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genetic interaction experiments in the results.

claim: Dorsal closure in the Drosophila embryo is an established model for epithelial morphogenesis.
source: Dorsal closure (DC) in the Drosophila embryo is an established model for epithelial morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Dorsal closure involves coordinated movements of two epithelial sheets: the epidermis and the amnioserosa.
source: The power of Drosophila genetics and cell biological tools have contributed to understand how signalling pathways, cell polarity and cell adhesion regulate the coordinated movements of two epithelial sheets, the epidermis and the amnioserosa (AS), a transient extraembryonic tissue [reviewed in (Ríos-Barrera and Riesgo-Escovar, 2013)].
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Dorsal closure is a complex morphogenetic process taking about 2 hours.
source: DC is a complex morphogenetic process taking about 2 hr, during which the epidermis expands dorsally to encompass the embryo.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Dorsal closure can be subdivided into three phases: elongation of dorsal-most epidermal cells, contraction of AS cells and migration of lateral epidermal cells, and zippering.
source: The process can be subdivided into three phases: i) elongation of the dorsal-most epidermal cells (DME) along the dorso-ventral axis; ii) contraction of AS cells and migration of the lateral epidermal cells towards the dorsal midline; iii) "zippering", i.e. adhesion of the epidermal cells from both sides on the dorsal midline [reviewed in (Gorfinkiel et al., 2011)].
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Pulsed contraction of AS cells produces a pulling force during dorsal closure.
source: First, pulsed contraction of AS cells produces a pulling force.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Pulsed contractions of AS cells are correlated with dynamic apical actomyosin foci.
source: These pulsed contractions are correlated with dynamic apical actomyosin foci, which transiently form in the apical medial cytocortex (Kiehart et al., 2000; Hutson et al., 2003; Solon et al., 2009; Gorfinkiel et al., 2009; Blanchard et al., 2010; Heisenberg and Bellaiche, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Cells delaminating from the AS contribute additional pulling forces during dorsal closure.
source: Cells delaminating from the AS contribute additional pulling forces (Muliyil et al., 2011; Sokolow et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: A supracellular actomyosin cable formed in the DME cells surrounds the opening and provides contractile forces during dorsal closure.
source: Second, a supracellular actomyosin cable, formed in the DME cells, surrounds the opening and provides contractile forces (Hutson et al., 2003; Rodriguez-Diaz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Zippering of the two lateral epithelial sheets is mediated by dynamic filopodia and lamellipodia.
source: Finally, "zippering" of the two lateral epithelial sheets occurs, mediated by dynamic filopodia and lamellipodia (Eltsov et al., 2015; Jacinto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Non-muscle myosin-II heavy chain and the non-muscle myosin regulatory light chain are part of a force-producing molecular motor during dorsal closure.
source: Non-muscle myosin-II heavy chain (MHC) and the non-muscle myosin regulatory light chain (MRLC), encoded by zipper (zip) and spaghetti-squash (sqh), respectively, are, together with the essential light chain, part of a force-producing molecular motor during DC [reviewed in (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Liu and Cheney, 2012)].
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Small G-proteins of the Rho family regulate actomyosin activity and cell-cell adhesion during dorsal closure.
source: The small G-proteins of the Rho family, namely Rho1, Rac1, Rac2, Mtl, and Cdc42, regulate actomyosin activity and cell-cell adhesion (Abreu-Blanco et al., 2014; Magie et al., 1999; 2002).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Rho GTPases stimulate myosin contraction through Rho-kinase (Rok).
source: These GTPases stimulate myosin contraction through Rho-kinase (Rok) (Mizuno et al., 1999; Harden et al., 1999) or p21-activated kinase (DPak) (Harden et al., 1996; Conder et al., 2004; Hofmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Rho GTPases stimulate myosin contraction through p21-activated kinase (DPak).
source: These GTPases stimulate myosin contraction through Rho-kinase (Rok) (Mizuno et al., 1999; Harden et al., 1999) or p21-activated kinase (DPak) (Harden et al., 1996; Conder et al., 2004; Hofmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex consists of seven subunits conserved in almost all eukaryotes.
source: They also modulate the Arp2/3 complex, which consists of seven subunits conserved in almost all eukaryotes (Rotty et al., 2013; Veltman and Insall, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex promotes the formation of densely branched, rapidly treadmilling actin filament arrays.
source: The Arp2/3 complex promotes the formation of densely branched, rapidly treadmilling actin filament arrays that, together with the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) and the WASP-family verprolin-homologous protein (WAVE), coordinate membrane-cytoskeleton dynamics (Lecuit et al., 2011; Kurisu and Takenawa, 2009; Blanchoin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex regulates endocytosis of DE-cadherin.
source: The Arp2/3 complex also regulates endocytosis of DE-cadherin (Georgiou et al., 2008; Leibfried et al., 2008) and thus contributes to the regulation of the zonula adherens (ZA), an adhesion belt encircling the apex of epithelial cells (Tepass et al., 1996; McEwen et al., 2000; Sarpal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The Drosophila WAVE homolog SCAR is the main activator of Arp2/3 in fly embryos.
source: Moreover, the Drosophila WAVE homolog SCAR, the main activator of Arp2/3 in fly embryos (Zallen et al., 2002), is a downstream effector of Rac, Cdc42 and DPak (Lecuit et al., 2011; Kurisu and Takenawa, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: DPak can activate the Arp2/3 complex independently of SCAR.
source: DPak, in turn, can also activate the Arp2/3 complex independently of SCAR (Lecuit et al., 2011; Kurisu and Takenawa, 2009; Zallen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The Crumbs protein complex is a key regulator of epithelial cell polarity in the Drosophila embryo.
source: One of the key regulators of epithelial cell polarity in the Drosophila embryo is the Crumbs protein complex.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The core components of the Crumbs complex are the type I transmembrane protein Crumbs (Crb) and the scaffolding proteins Stardust (Sdt), DLin-7 and DPATJ.
source: Its core components are the type I transmembrane protein Crumbs (Crb) and the scaffolding proteins Stardust (Sdt), DLin-7 and DPATJ, which are conserved from flies to mammals [reviewed in (Bulgakova and Knust, 2009; Tepass, 2012)].
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Drosophila embryos mutant for crb or sdt are unable to maintain apico-basal polarity in most of their epithelia.
source: Drosophila embryos mutant for crb or sdt are unable to maintain apico-basal polarity in most of their epithelia (Tepass and Knust, 1990; 1993; Bachmann et al., 2001; Hong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Loss of crb or sdt leads to a complete breakdown of tissue integrity due to failure in positioning and maintaining the ZA, followed by apoptosis in many tissues.
source: This leads to a complete breakdown of tissue integrity due to failure in positioning and maintaining the ZA, followed by apoptosis in many tissues, e.g. the epidermis and the AS (Grawe et al., 1996; Tepass and Knust, 1990; 1993; Tepass, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Mice lacking Crb2 or Crb3 show comparable defects in epithelial integrity to Drosophila crb mutants.
source: Comparable defects in epithelial integrity are observed in mice lacking Crb2 or Crb3 (Whiteman et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2011; Szymaniak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Over-expression of Drosophila Crb can lead to an expansion of the apical membrane domain in embryonic epithelial cells and photoreceptor cells.
source: Conversely, over-expression of Drosophila Crb can lead to an expansion of the apical membrane domain, both in embryonic epithelial cells (Wodarz et al., 1995) and in photoreceptor cells (Muschalik and Knust, 2011; Pellikka et al., 2002; Richard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Crb is an important apical determinant of epithelial cells.
source: These results define Crb as an important apical determinant of epithelial cells.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from previous results cited in the introduction.

claim: Drosophila crb controls tissue size in imaginal discs by acting upstream of the Hippo pathway.
source: Besides a role in epithelial cell polarity, Drosophila crb controls tissue size in imaginal discs by acting upstream of the Hippo pathway [reviewed in (Boggiano and Fehon, 2012; Genevet and Tapon, 2011)], regulates morphogenesis of photoreceptor cells and prevents light-dependent retinal degeneration [reviewed in (Bazellières et al., 2009; Bulgakova and Knust, 2009)].
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Crb regulates morphogenesis of photoreceptor cells and prevents light-dependent retinal degeneration.
source: Besides a role in epithelial cell polarity, Drosophila crb controls tissue size in imaginal discs by acting upstream of the Hippo pathway [reviewed in (Boggiano and Fehon, 2012; Genevet and Tapon, 2011)], regulates morphogenesis of photoreceptor cells and prevents light-dependent retinal degeneration [reviewed in (Bazellières et al., 2009; Bulgakova and Knust, 2009)].
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The cytoplasmic portion of Crb contains a C-terminal PDZ domain-binding motif (PBM) -ERLI.
source: Its small cytoplasmic portion of only 37 amino acids contains two highly conserved motifs, a C-terminal PDZ (Postsynaptic density/Discs large/ZO-1) domain-binding motif (PBM), -ERLI, which can bind the PDZ-domain of Sdt and DPar-6 (Li et al., 2014; Roh et al., 2002; Bulgakova et al., 2008; Bachmann et al., 2001; Hong et al., 2001; Kempkens et al., 2006; Ivanova et al., 2015), and a FERM (protein 4.1/ezrin/radixin/moesin) domain-binding motif (FBM) (Klebes and Knust, 2000), which can directly interact with the FERM-domain of Yurt (Yrt), Expanded (Ex) and Moesin (Moe) (Laprise et al., 2006; Ling et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The PBM of Crb can bind the PDZ-domain of Sdt and DPar-6.
source: Its small cytoplasmic portion of only 37 amino acids contains two highly conserved motifs, a C-terminal PDZ (Postsynaptic density/Discs large/ZO-1) domain-binding motif (PBM), -ERLI, which can bind the PDZ-domain of Sdt and DPar-6 (Li et al., 2014; Roh et al., 2002; Bulgakova et al., 2008; Bachmann et al., 2001; Hong et al., 2001; Kempkens et al., 2006; Ivanova et al., 2015), and a FERM (protein 4.1/ezrin/radixin/moesin) domain-binding motif (FBM) (Klebes and Knust, 2000), which can directly interact with the FERM-domain of Yurt (Yrt), Expanded (Ex) and Moesin (Moe) (Laprise et al., 2006; Ling et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The FBM of Crb can directly interact with the FERM-domain of Yurt (Yrt), Expanded (Ex) and Moesin (Moe).
source: Its small cytoplasmic portion of only 37 amino acids contains two highly conserved motifs, a C-terminal PDZ (Postsynaptic density/Discs large/ZO-1) domain-binding motif (PBM), -ERLI, which can bind the PDZ-domain of Sdt and DPar-6 (Li et al., 2014; Roh et al., 2002; Bulgakova et al., 2008; Bachmann et al., 2001; Hong et al., 2001; Kempkens et al., 2006; Ivanova et al., 2015), and a FERM (protein 4.1/ezrin/radixin/moesin) domain-binding motif (FBM) (Klebes and Knust, 2000), which can directly interact with the FERM-domain of Yurt (Yrt), Expanded (Ex) and Moesin (Moe) (Laprise et al., 2006; Ling et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The PBM of Crb is essential for the maintenance of cell polarity in embryonic epithelia.
source: Our previous structure-function analysis of Crb using a fosmid-based approach revealed that the PBM is essential for the maintenance of cell polarity in embryonic epithelia (Klose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: The FBM of Crb is non-essential for normal development of most embryonic epithelia.
source: In contrast, the FBM is non-essential for normal development of most embryonic epithelia.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding.

claim: Embryos with a mutation in the FBM of Crb fail to undergo dorsal closure at later stages of development.
source: At later stages of development, however, embryos with a mutation in the FBM fail to undergo DC (Klose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: A fosmid covering the entire crb locus (foscrb) completely rescues the lethality caused by the lack of endogenous crb.
source: We previously showed (Klose et al., 2013) that a fosmid covering the entire crb locus, named foscrb, completely rescues the lethality caused by the lack of endogenous crb.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: The foscrbY10A variant does not rescue embryonic lethality.
source: We also showed that a variant, in which the conserved tyrosine10 in the FERM-domain binding motif (FBM) is replaced by an alanine (foscrbY10A variant) does not rescue embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: The fosCrbY10A variant properly localises at the apical domain in most embryonic epithelia, which undergo normal morphogenesis.
source: Interestingly, the fosCrbY10A variant properly localises at the apical domain in most embryonic epithelia, which undergo normal morphogenesis (i.e. germ band elongation, salivary gland invagination).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos, germ band retraction, dorsal closure and head involution fail to occur properly.
source: But later in development, germ band (GB) retraction, dorsal closure (DC) and head involution fail to occur properly (Klose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: The FBM of Crb fulfils a tissue- and stage-specific morphogenetic function in the embryo.
source: This indicated that the FBM of Crb fulfils a tissue- and stage-specific morphogenetic function in the embryo.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from previous findings.

claim: The defects in foscrbY10A embryos appear to be independent of a putative Tyr phosphorylation.
source: Moreover, these defects appear to be independent of a putative Tyr phosphorylation, because another variant, in which the Y10 is replaced by a phenylalanine (foscrbY10F), completely rescues the embryonic lethality of crb mutants (Klose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: By the time foscrb embryos finish GB retraction, foscrbY10A embryos exhibit major defects in GB retraction.
source: By the time foscrb embryos finish GB retraction (Figure 1A, Video 1), foscrbY10A embryos (Figure 1B, Video 2) exhibit major defects in GB retraction, as revealed by a highly disorganised amnioserosa (AS) in which individual AS cells could hardly be followed.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: While foscrb embryos proceed through DC, foscrbY10A embryos progressively lose the AS and ultimately fail to complete DC.
source: While foscrb embryos proceed through DC (Figure 1C,E, Video 1), those expressing the foscrbY10A variant progressively lose the AS (Figure 1D,F) and ultimately fail to complete DC (Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Embryos expressing the foscrbY10F variant complete DC similar to foscrb embryos.
source: Embryos expressing the foscrbY10F variant complete DC similar as foscrb embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the Y10A mutation specifically affects the progress of DC.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Y10A mutation specifically affects the progress of DC.
source: Embryos expressing the foscrbY10F variant complete DC similar as foscrb embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the Y10A mutation specifically affects the progress of DC.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of foscrbY10F and foscrbY10A phenotypes.

claim: Elongation of the dorsal most epidermal (DME) cells occurs normally in foscrb embryos.
source: This elongation occurs normally in foscrb embryos, as revealed by phosphotyrosine (PY) staining associated with the ZA (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The DME cells of foscrbY10A embryos do not elongate co-ordinately.
source: In contrast the DME cells of foscrbY10A embryos do not elongate co-ordinately (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In foscrb embryos, Crb and DPatj are mostly absent from the leading edge (LE) of the DME cells.
source: In foscrb embryos, Crb (Figure 1I) and DPatj (Figure 1I') are mostly absent from the leading edge (LE –Figure 1I–I' arrowheads) of the DME cells.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I-I'.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos, both CrbY10A and DPatj are detected at the LE, particularly in those cells that remain short.
source: In contrast, in foscrbY10A embryos both CrbY10A (Figure 1J, asterisks) and DPatj (Figure 1J', asterisks) are detected at the LE, particularly in those cells that remain short, while both are removed in cells that elongate properly (Figure 1J,J', arrowheads).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1J-J'.

claim: Proper elongation of the DME cells fails in foscrbY10A embryos.
source: Thus proper elongation of the DME cells fails in foscrbY10A embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of DME cell morphology and protein localization.

claim: Filopodia extend dorsally in foscrb embryos.
source: These filopodia, revealed by staining with an antibody against Stranded at Second [Sas (Denholm et al., 2005)], extend dorsally in foscrb embryos (Figure 2A arrow).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Filopodia in foscrbY10A embryos are disorganised and often absent.
source: In contrast, filopodia in foscrbY10A embryos are disorganised and often absent (Figure 2B, empty arrowhead and arrowhead, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Filopodia of foscrbY10A embryos are erratic, and some even appear to move out of the plane.
source: Filopodia of foscrbY10A embryos are erratic, and some even appear to move out of the plane (Video 3, arrow in foscrbY10A embryo), probably because of the loss of contact with the AS.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Video 3.

claim: Enabled (Ena) is a key regulator of the number and length of filopodia during DC.
source: A key regulator of the number and length of filopodia during DC is the actin-elongation promoting protein Enabled (Ena) (Gates et al., 2007; Nowotarski et al., 2014; Bilancia et al., 2014; Homem and Peifer, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Ena concentrates at the LE of DME cells in foscrb embryos.
source: Ena concentrates at the LE of DME cells in foscrb embryos (Figure 2C, arrows).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ena is strongly reduced at the LE of foscrbY10A embryos.
source: In contrast, Ena is strongly reduced at the LE of foscrbY10A embryos (Figure 2D, arrowhead).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Pyd localisation at the ZA shows no major difference in foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos.
source: However, Pyd localisation at the ZA shows no major difference in foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B''').
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B'''.

claim: The localisation of the formins Dia and DAAM is similar in foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos.
source: The localisation of the formins Dia and DAAM, both involved in the growth of actin-based protrusions (Matusek et al., 2006; Homem and Peifer, 2008; Liu et al., 2010), is also similar in foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Different regulators of Ena are affected in foscrbY10A mutant embryos.
source: This suggests that different regulators of Ena are affected in foscrbY10A mutant embryos.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Pyd, Dia, and DAAM localization are normal while Ena is reduced.

claim: The supracellular actomyosin cable is correctly formed in foscrb embryos.
source: This supracellular cable, which contains actin (Figure 2E) and the non-muscle myosin II Zipper (Zip, Figure 2E'), is correctly formed in foscrb embryos (Figure 2E,E' arrows).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E,E'.

claim: The supracellular actomyosin cable is virtually absent in foscrbY10A embryos.
source: However, it is virtually absent in foscrbY10A embryos (Figure 2F,F', arrowheads).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2F,F'.

claim: Zip::GFP appears homogenously along the LE in foscrb embryos.
source: Live imaging experiments using a zipper::GFP protein trap line (Buszczak et al., 2007; Morin et al., 2001) reveal that Zip::GFP appears homogenously along the LE in foscrb embryos.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Zip::GFP randomly concentrates in some segments along the LE of foscrbY10A embryos.
source: In contrast, it randomly concentrates in some segments along the LE of foscrbY10A embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The FBM of Crb is important for the generation and maintenance of actin-based protrusions and the correct organisation of the supracellular actomyosin cable at the LE.
source: Together, these results show that the FBM of Crb is important for the generation and maintenance of actin-based protrusions and the correct organisation of the supracellular actomyosin cable at the LE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of filopodia and actomyosin cable defects.

claim: The formation of the actomyosin cable at the LE depends on the removal of the adhesion protein Echinoid (Ed) from the LE and the AS cells.
source: The formation of the actomyosin cable at the LE depends on the removal of the adhesion protein Echinoid (Ed) from the LE and the AS cells (Laplante and Nilson, 2011; Lin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Ed in foscrb embryos is distributed as in wild type embryos.
source: As expected, Ed in foscrb embryos is distributed as in wild type embryos (Figure 2G, arrowheads mark Ed absence at the LE).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos, Ed levels are strongly reduced in the DME cells.
source: However, in foscrbY10A embryos, Ed levels are strongly reduced in the DME cells (Figure 2H, magenta overlay), even though the DME cells are still in contact with the AS, as revealed by PY staining (Figure 2H').
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2H,H'.

claim: The asymmetric distribution of Ed is essential to exclude the polarity protein Bazooka (Baz) away from the LE.
source: It has been suggested that the asymmetric distribution of Ed is essential to exclude the polarity protein Bazooka (Baz) away from the LE (Laplante and Nilson, 2011; Pickering et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: foscrbY10A embryos preserve Baz at the LE of those cells that fail to elongate.
source: We found that, in contrast to foscrb embryos (Figure 2I, arrowhead), foscrbY10A embryos preserve Baz at the LE of those cells that fail to elongate (Figure 2J, arrow).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I,J.

claim: There is a general reduction of Baz at the junctions of the DME cells of foscrbY10A embryos.
source: In addition, there is a general reduction of Baz at the junctions of the DME cells of foscrbY10A embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The FBM of Crb is important for Ed stability and hence Baz redistribution and amount in DME cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that the FBM of Crb is important for Ed stability and hence Baz redistribution and amount in DME cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of Ed and Baz localization defects.

claim: Removal of Coracle (Cora), Discs Large (Dlg) and Yurt (Yrt) from the LE appears normal in the different fosmid variants.
source: We found that removal of Coracle (Cora), Discs Large (Dlg) and Yurt (Yrt) from the LE appears normal in the different fosmid variants (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that not all aspects of the planar polarisation of the DME cells are affected in embryos expressing the foscrbY10A variant.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Not all aspects of the planar polarisation of the DME cells are affected in embryos expressing the foscrbY10A variant.
source: We found that removal of Coracle (Cora), Discs Large (Dlg) and Yurt (Yrt) from the LE appears normal in the different fosmid variants (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that not all aspects of the planar polarisation of the DME cells are affected in embryos expressing the foscrbY10A variant.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that septate junction components are properly removed.

claim: In foscrb embryos, DE-cad localises at all cell-cell contacts, including the LE.
source: In foscrb, DE-cad localises at all cell-cell contacts, including the LE (Figure 2K, arrow).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos, the DE-cad signal is strongly reduced at the LE.
source: In foscrbY10A embryos, however, the DE-cad signal is strongly reduced at the LE (Figure 2L, solid arrowhead).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Disruption of DE-cad suggests a discontinuous adhesion belt in the AS cells of foscrbY10A embryos.
source: Moreover, disruption of DE-cad suggests a discontinuous adhesion belt in the AS cells of these embryos (Figure 2L, empty arrowheads).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The loss of DE-cad from the LE in the foscrbY10A embryos at this early stage is different from the normal redistribution of DE-cad that occurs at late stages during the zippering phase.
source: The loss of DE-cad from the LE in the foscrbY10A embryos at this early stage is different from the normal redistribution of DE-cad that occurs at late stages during the zippering phase (Gorfinkiel and Arias, 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously reported normal developmental processes.

claim: In foscrbY10F embryos, all proteins mentioned above localise as in foscrb embryos.
source: As expected, in foscrbY10F embryos, all proteins mentioned above localise as in foscrb embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The DC phenotype in foscrbY10A embryos is accompanied by defects in the establishment of the complex actomyosin apparatus at the LE of the DME cells and by the disturbance or even loss of different components of the ZA.
source: Taken together, these results show that the DC phenotype in foscrbY10A embryos is accompanied by defects in the establishment of the complex actomyosin apparatus at the LE of the DME cells and by the disturbance or even loss of different components of the ZA (schematised in Figure 2M,N).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from multiple observations.

claim: At the beginning of stage 11, AS cells are elongated along the antero-posterior axis in foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos.
source: In foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos, at the beginning of stage 11, AS cells are elongated along the antero-posterior axis (Figure 3A,D), highlighted by DE-cad::mTomato along the ZA (Figure 3B,E, arrows).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B,D,E.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos, the continuity of DE-cad::mTomato is frequently disrupted.
source: In foscrbY10A embryos, however, the continuity of DE-cad::mTomato is frequently disrupted (Figure 3E, arrowhead) and DE-cad::mTomato additionally appears in large intracellular clusters of unknown identity (Figure 3E, concave arrowheads), which are never observed in foscrb embryos.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: As GB retraction proceeds, fragmentation of the ZA continues in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos and the tissue disintegrates.
source: As GB retraction proceeds, fragmentation of the ZA continues in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos and the tissue disintegrates (Figure 3F arrowheads and Video 4; and for a dorsal view of a different set of embryos see Video 5), while the dorsal aspect of foscrb embryos is covered by a continuous epithelial sheet (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3C,F and Videos 4 and 5.

claim: At stage 14, the AS forms a flat monolayer of epithelial cells in foscrb embryos.
source: At stage 14, the AS forms a flat monolayer of epithelial cells in foscrb embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,A').
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,A'.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos developed for the same period of time, the AS is completely disorganised.
source: In contrast, in foscrbY10A embryos developed for the same period of time, the AS is completely disorganised.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,B'.

claim: Cell-cell adhesion in the AS is strongly disrupted in foscrbY10A embryos.
source: Together, these observations suggest that cell-cell adhesion in the AS is strongly disrupted in foscrbY10A embryos, and define the FBM of Crb as an important regulator of cytoskeletal organisation and cell-cell adhesion of the AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple observations of AS morphology and DE-cad localization.

claim: The FBM of Crb is an important regulator of cytoskeletal organisation and cell-cell adhesion of the AS.
source: Together, these observations suggest that cell-cell adhesion in the AS is strongly disrupted in foscrbY10A embryos, and define the FBM of Crb as an important regulator of cytoskeletal organisation and cell-cell adhesion of the AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple observations.

claim: In foscrb embryos, some apoptotic cells are visible at the posterior canthus at the end of GB retraction.
source: Apoliner expression in the AS (specifically driven by the line GAL4332.3) of foscrb embryos (Video 6) revealed some apoptotic cells at the posterior canthus at the end of GB retraction (Figure 4A, arrow).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A and Video 6.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos developed for the same period of time, more apoptotic cells are visible, some of which detach.
source: In foscrbY10A embryos developed for the same period of time, more apoptotic cells are visible, some of which detach (Figure 4B, arrowheads), while others remain attached to the posterior edge of the remaining AS (Figure 4B, arrow).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Video 6.

claim: As DC progresses in foscrb embryos, some apoptotic cells delaminate from the AS.
source: As DC progresses in foscrb embryos, some apoptotic cells delaminate from the AS and are easily distinguished (Video 6, blinking arrows –some of these cells could be hemocytes with engulfed apoptotic debris, as reported previously [Bardet et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Video 6, with speculation about cell identity.

claim: At advanced DC stage, almost all AS cells in foscrbY10A embryos are apoptotic.
source: At this stage, almost all AS cells in foscrbY10A embryos are apoptotic (Video 6, compare embryos at 210 min).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Video 6.

claim: At the end of DC, the internalised AS cells are localised in a central rod-like structure in foscrb embryos and subsequently die by apoptosis.
source: Finally, at the end of DC, the internalised AS cells are localised in a central rod-like structure in foscrb embryos and subsequently die by apoptosis (Figure 4C) [as has been reported for wild type embryos (Reed et al., 2004; Shen et al., 2013)], while in foscrbY10A embryos at this time point the remaining AS cells are completely disaggregated (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4C,D, with citation to previous reports.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos at the end of DC, the remaining AS cells are completely disaggregated.
source: Finally, at the end of DC, the internalised AS cells are localised in a central rod-like structure in foscrb embryos and subsequently die by apoptosis (Figure 4C) [as has been reported for wild type embryos (Reed et al., 2004; Shen et al., 2013)], while in foscrbY10A embryos at this time point the remaining AS cells are completely disaggregated (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The AS in foscrbY10A embryos breaks apart and undergoes premature apoptosis.
source: To summarise, the AS in foscrbY10A embryos breaks apart and undergoes premature apoptosis (Video 6), supporting the conclusion that an intact FBM is required for maintaining the integrity of the AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the apoptosis observations.

claim: An intact FBM is required for maintaining the integrity of the AS.
source: To summarise, the AS in foscrbY10A embryos breaks apart and undergoes premature apoptosis (Video 6), supporting the conclusion that an intact FBM is required for maintaining the integrity of the AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of AS disintegration and apoptosis.

claim: There is no significant difference in the number of β–gal positive nuclei at middle DC along 50 μm at the dorsal epidermis between foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos.
source: However, given that there is no significant difference in the number of β-gal positive nuclei along 50 μm of the dorsal epidermis between these genotypes (Figure 4G,H, brackets and 4K), we suggest that this phenotype is the result of aberrant elongation of the DME cells in foscrbY10A embryos (see for example Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by quantification shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The phenotype of β–gal positive cells below DME cells in foscrbY10A embryos is the result of aberrant elongation of the DME cells.
source: However, given that there is no significant difference in the number of β-gal positive nuclei along 50 μm of the dorsal epidermis between these genotypes (Figure 4G,H, brackets and 4K), we suggest that this phenotype is the result of aberrant elongation of the DME cells in foscrbY10A embryos (see for example Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference from the quantification and morphological observations.

claim: At the time when foscrb embryos complete DC, foscrb and foscrbY10A embryos exhibit a single row of β-gal positive cells on each side of the dorsal epidermis.
source: Accordingly, at the time when foscrb embryos complete DC, these embryos (Figure 4I) and foscrbY10A embryos exhibit a single row of β-gal positive cells on each side of the dorsal epidermis (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I,J.

claim: A normal activation of JNK signalling is observed in foscrbY10F embryos.
source: A normal activation of JNK signalling is also observed in foscrbY10F embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), showing that JNK signalling appears to be normal in the DME cells of foscrbY10A embryos.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: JNK signalling appears to be normal in the DME cells of foscrbY10A embryos.
source: A normal activation of JNK signalling is also observed in foscrbY10F embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), showing that JNK signalling appears to be normal in the DME cells of foscrbY10A embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the puc-lacZ reporter expression pattern.

claim: The FBM of Crb is an important regulator of the integrity and morphogenesis of the AS without affecting its specification during development.
source: Taken together, these results support the conclusion that the FBM of Crb is an important regulator of the integrity and morphogenesis of the AS without affecting its specification during development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple observations including Hnt expression, integrin localization, and JNK signaling.

claim: Perturbing actomyosin dynamics of the AS cells interferes with normal DC.
source: It has been previously shown that perturbing actomyosin dynamics of the AS cells interferes with normal DC (Solon et al., 2009; Gorfinkiel et al., 2009; Fischer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Actomyosin dynamics in stage 13 foscrb embryos is characterised by pulsed contractions of the AS cells.
source: These dynamics, which are evident in stage 13 foscrb embryos (Video 8) similar as in wild-type embryos, is characterised by pulsed contractions of the AS cells.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Video 8.

claim: In foscrbY10A embryos, the pulsed contraction are difficult to follow, since individual cells can hardly be distinguished due to the highly disrupted ZA.
source: In foscrbY10A embryos, however, the pulsed contraction are difficult to follow, since individual cells can hardly be distinguished due to the highly disrupted ZA (Video 8, compare Figure 5A and 5B).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Video 8 and Figure 5A,B.

claim: Pulsed-contraction of wild-type AS cells has been correlated with a regular appearance and disappearance of medial actomyosin foci.
source: Pulsed-contraction of wild-type AS cells has been correlated with a regular appearance and disappearance of medial actomyosin foci (Blanchard et al., 2010; David et al., 2010; Solon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Actomyosin foci in foscrb embryos are transient and disassemble after contraction.
source: These actomyosin foci are observed in foscrb embryos as revealed by Zip::GFP (Video 9 and Figure 5C). Kymographs show that these foci are transient and disassemble after contraction (Figure 5C',D').
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Video 9 and Figure 5C,C'.

claim: The AS of foscrbY10A embryos shows more Zip::GFP foci, some of which are more prominent.
source: In contrast, the AS of foscrbY10A embryos shows more Zip::GFP foci (Figure 5D), some of which are more prominent (Figure 5D', and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 10).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5D,D' and Video 10.

claim: foscrb and foscrbY10F embryos have similar pulsed contractions, while foscrbY10A embryos have aberrant contractions, in that foci are more persistent.
source: Importantly, analysis of the periodicity of foci formation shows that foscrb and foscrbY10F embryos have similar pulsed contractions, while foscrbY10A embryos have aberrant contractions, in that foci are more persistent (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The AS of embryos expressing the CrbY10A variant is under both constant and uncoordinated contraction.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that the AS of embryos expressing the CrbY10A variant is under both constant and uncoordinated contraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of actomyosin foci dynamics.

claim: Expressing Flapwing (flw) in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos leads to a suppression of the DC phenotype.
source: In fact, UAS-driven expression of Flw in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos leads to a suppression of the DC phenotype (Figure 6D–F, Video 11), while it does not produce any evident dominant phenotype in foscrb or foscrbY10F embryos (Figure 6A–C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Video 11.

claim: Flw over-expression suppresses the disruption of the ZA in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos.
source: Interestingly, Flw over-expression also suppresses the disruption of the ZA in the AS (Video 12, compare B vs. D).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Video 12.

claim: The FBM of Crb negatively regulates actomyosin activity in the AS.
source: This result supports our hypothesis that the FBM of Crb negatively regulates actomyosin activity in the AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Flw over-expression rescue experiment.

claim: Heterozygosity of Rho11B partially suppresses the DC phenotype of foscrbY10A embryos.
source: Our data suggest that Rho1 plays a crucial role downstream of Crb, since heterozygosity of Rho11B partially suppresses the DC phenotype of foscrbY10A embryos.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Over-expression of dominant-negative Rho (RhoN19) in the AS of foscrbY10A increases the number of hatched larvae.
source: In line with this conclusion we found that over-expression of dominant-negative Rho (RhoN19) or a kinase-dead Rok (Rok-CAT-KG) in the AS of foscrbY10A increases the number of hatched larvae (Figure 7A, 5th vs. 12th and 13th gray bars: from 2.9% to 13.4% and 10.0%, respectively), and the proportion of embryos with open cuticles is reduced (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, 5th vs 12th and 13th black bars, from 52.7% to 23.6% and 28.5%, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over-expression of kinase-dead Rok (Rok-CAT-KG) in the AS of foscrbY10A increases the number of hatched larvae.
source: In line with this conclusion we found that over-expression of dominant-negative Rho (RhoN19) or a kinase-dead Rok (Rok-CAT-KG) in the AS of foscrbY10A increases the number of hatched larvae (Figure 7A, 5th vs. 12th and 13th gray bars: from 2.9% to 13.4% and 10.0%, respectively), and the proportion of embryos with open cuticles is reduced (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, 5th vs 12th and 13th black bars, from 52.7% to 23.6% and 28.5%, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over-expression of the auto-inhibitory domain of DPak (DPak-AID) in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos leads to a very strong suppression of the DC phenotype.
source: Interestingly, over-expression of the auto-inhibitory domain of DPak [DPak-AID -(Conder et al., 2004)] in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos leads to a very strong suppression of the DC phenotype, as 59% of those embryos hatch (Figure 7A, 17th vs. 6th bars), and even adult flies eclose (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A and adult fly images in Figure 7D.

claim: Over-expression of constitutive active DPak (DPak-myr) in the AS of otherwise viable foscrb embryos leads to embryonic lethality with >90% of embryos with a DC-defect.
source: Accordingly, over-expression of constitutive active DPak (DPak-myr) in the AS of otherwise viable foscrb embryos leads to embryonic lethality with >90% of embryos with a DC-defect (Figure 7A, 18th vs. 19th bars).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Unregulated activation of DPak in the AS is sufficient to produce defects in DC.
source: These results indicate that unregulated activation of DPak in the AS is sufficient to produce defects in DC, and that this kinase plays a major role in the defects observed in the foscrbY10A embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DPak gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: DPak plays a major role in the defects observed in the foscrbY10A embryos.
source: These results indicate that unregulated activation of DPak in the AS is sufficient to produce defects in DC, and that this kinase plays a major role in the defects observed in the foscrbY10A embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DPak genetic interaction experiments.

claim: The FBM of Crb can recruit DMoesin (DMoe) to the membrane.
source: The participation of DMoe in the process under discussion here is supported by the fact that the FBM of Crb can recruit DMoesin (DMoe) to the membrane (Médina et al., 2002) and physically interacts with it (Wei et al., 2015), and that phosphorylated-DMoe (P-DMoe) is reduced in stage 11 foscrbY10A embryos (Klose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: The FBM of Crb physically interacts with DMoesin.
source: The participation of DMoe in the process under discussion here is supported by the fact that the FBM of Crb can recruit DMoesin (DMoe) to the membrane (Médina et al., 2002) and physically interacts with it (Wei et al., 2015), and that phosphorylated-DMoe (P-DMoe) is reduced in stage 11 foscrbY10A embryos (Klose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Phosphorylated-DMoe (P-DMoe) is reduced in stage 11 foscrbY10A embryos.
source: The participation of DMoe in the process under discussion here is supported by the fact that the FBM of Crb can recruit DMoesin (DMoe) to the membrane (Médina et al., 2002) and physically interacts with it (Wei et al., 2015), and that phosphorylated-DMoe (P-DMoe) is reduced in stage 11 foscrbY10A embryos (Klose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citation support.

claim: The reduction in P-DMoe persists during DC in foscrbY10A embryos.
source: This reduction in P-DMoe persists during DC (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Over-expression of the phosphomimetic form DMoeT559D in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos notably increases the number of larvae that hatch.
source: In line with this, over-expression of the phosphomimetic form DMoeT559D in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos notably increases the number of larvae that hatch (Figure 7A, 6th vs. 20th gray bars, from 10.8% to 30.9%), while over-expression of DMoe does not ameliorate the DC defects in those embryos (Figure 7A, 21st bar).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Over-expression of DMoe does not ameliorate the DC defects in foscrbY10A embryos.
source: In line with this, over-expression of the phosphomimetic form DMoeT559D in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos notably increases the number of larvae that hatch (Figure 7A, 6th vs. 20th gray bars, from 10.8% to 30.9%), while over-expression of DMoe does not ameliorate the DC defects in those embryos (Figure 7A, 21st bar).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The regulation of the cytoskeleton dynamics by Crb is mediated in part by the active form of DMoe.
source: This suggests that the regulation of the cytoskeleton dynamics by Crb is mediated in part by the active form of DMoe.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DMoe genetic interaction experiments.

claim: The FBM of Crb regulates actomyosin dynamics in the AS during DC by down-regulating the activity of the Rho1 pathway.
source: Together these results let us to conclude, that the FBM of Crb regulates actomyosin dynamics in the AS during DC by down-regulating the activity of the Rho1 pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Driving the expression of UAS-CrbWT in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos leads to a suppression of the DC phenotype.
source: Driving the expression of UAS-CrbWT in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos leads to a suppression of the DC phenotype, as >36% hatch at 18ºC (Figure 7A, 8th and 9th bars vs. 5th gray bars), while inducing a stronger over-expression by maintaining embryos at 29°C does not ameliorate the foscrbY10A phenotype (Figure 7A, 5th vs. 7th bars).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The DC phenotype of foscrbY10A embryos is due to loss of Crb function.
source: These results show that the DC phenotype of foscrbY10A embryos is due to loss of Crb function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment with wild-type Crb.

claim: Over-expression of DE-cad in the AS of foscrbY10A embryos can suppress the DC phenotype.
source: Over-expression of DE-cad in the AS of these embryos indeed can suppress the DC phenotype, as 70% of the larvae hatched (Figure 7A, 22nd vs. 6th bars), and even adult animals are obtained (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A and adult fly images in Figure 7E.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex regulates endocytosis of DE-cad.
source: A likely candidate of DE-cad regulation is the Arp2/3 complex, which has been shown to regulate endocytosis of DE-cad (Georgiou et al., 2008; Leibfried et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: Reducing the activity of the Arp2/3 complex suppresses the DC phenotype of α-Cat mutants.
source: In addition, reducing the activity of the Arp2/3 complex suppresses the DC phenotype of α-Cat mutants (Sarpal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation support.

claim: foscrbY10A embryos that are heterozygous for SCAR∆37 exhibit only minor defects in GB retraction.
source: Strikingly, foscrbY10A embryos that are heterozygous for SCAR∆37 exhibit only minor defects in GB retraction (Figure 8B), partially restore DE-cad::GFP localisation in the AS (compare Figure 8H with Figure 5B) and completed DC (Figure 8F, Video 13).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8 and Video 13.

claim: foscrbY10A embryos heterozygous for SCAR∆37 partially restore DE-cad::GFP localisation in the AS.
source: Strikingly, foscrbY10A embryos that are heterozygous for SCAR∆37 exhibit only minor defects in GB retraction (Figure 8B), partially restore DE-cad::GFP localisation in the AS (compare Figure 8H with Figure 5B) and completed DC (Figure 8F, Video 13).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8.

claim: foscrbY10A embryos heterozygous for SCAR∆37 completed DC.
source: Strikingly, foscrbY10A embryos that are heterozygous for SCAR∆37 exhibit only minor defects in GB retraction (Figure 8B), partially restore DE-cad::GFP localisation in the AS (compare Figure 8H with Figure 5B) and completed DC (Figure 8F, Video 13).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8F and Video 13.

claim: ~28% of foscrbY10A embryos heterozygous for SCAR∆37 hatch.
source: In fact, ~28% of these larvae hatch, as revealed by the cuticle phenotype (Figure 7A, 23rd vs. 2nd bar), and even some of the w;foscrbY10A,DE-cad::GFP/SCAR∆37,DE-cad::GFP;crbGX24 develop into adult flies that exhibit defects in abdominal development (Figure 7F, arrowhead).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Some foscrbY10A embryos heterozygous for SCAR∆37 develop into adult flies that exhibit defects in abdominal development.
source: In fact, ~28% of these larvae hatch, as revealed by the cuticle phenotype (Figure 7A, 23rd vs. 2nd bar), and even some of the w;foscrbY10A,DE-cad::GFP/SCAR∆37,DE-cad::GFP;crbGX24 develop into adult flies that exhibit defects in abdominal development (Figure 7F, arrowhead).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by adult fly images shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A similar suppression was obtained in foscrbY10A embryos heterozygous for Arp3EP3640.
source: A similar suppression was obtained in foscrbY10A embryos heterozygous for Arp3EP3640 (Video 14) (Figure 7A, 24th vs. 3rd bar).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by cuticle phenotype data shown in Figure 7A and Video 14.

claim: foscrb embryos heterozygous for SCAR∆37 or Arp3EP3640 show normal DC.
source: foscrb embryos heterozygous for SCAR∆37 or Arp3EP3640 show normal DC (Figure 8E and Video 14).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8E and Video 14.

claim: The DC phenotype of embryos expressing CrbY10A is due to enhanced Rho-mediated actomyosin activity and reduced adhesion.
source: In summary we could demonstrate that the DC phenotype of embryos expressing CrbY10A is due to enhanced Rho-mediated actomyosin activity and reduced adhesion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from multiple genetic interaction experiments.

claim: A mutation in the FERM-domain binding motif of the polarity determinant Crb affects major steps during DC, namely elongation of the DME cells, proper formation of the actomyosin cable at the LE, and regulated constriction of the AS cells.
source: Here we present data to show that a mutation in the FERM-domain binding motif of the polarity determinant Crb affects major steps during DC, namely elongation of the DME cells, proper formation of the actomyosin cable at the LE, and regulated constriction of the AS cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Impaired DE-cad localisation suggest impaired adhesion in foscrbY10A embryos.
source: In addition, impaired DE-cad localisation suggest impaired adhesion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DE-cad localization observations.

claim: The results define a novel role of the FBM of Crb as an essential negative regulator of actomyosin dynamics in the AS during DC in Drosophila.
source: Overall, our results define a novel role of the FBM of Crb as an essential negative regulator of actomyosin dynamics in the AS during DC in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion.

claim: This function of the FBM is mediated by DMoesin, members of the Rho family, the p21 activated kinase DPak, and the SCAR-Arp2/3 complex.
source: Genetic interaction studies revealed that this function of the FBM is mediated by DMoesin, members of the Rho family, the p21 activated kinase DPak, and the SCAR-Arp2/3 complex (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the genetic interaction results.
